This change introduces generating definitions corresponding to
`*-map` property, which was currently discarded.

The `*-map` data is like a two-dimensional array, so it is difficult to
handle with the existing APIs, so we will also provide new APIs.

---

Common utilities have been separated into a separate PR.
Please take a look at this first. https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/84190


---

I noticed this problem while developing https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/gsoc-2022-arduino-core.

Since map is used to associate with the physical layout, there is a need to know the "physical pin names".

Since the mapping process is performed during the generation of devicetree-generated.h, I don't think there are many cases where information about the mapping source is needed. However, there are such cases, however rare, and it is not desirable for the information written in the devicetree to be discarded, so I would like to introduce this.

title: drivers: counter: introduce counter capture api
labels: area: Counter;platform: STM32;area: Devicetree Binding;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
This introduces apis for input capture on the STM32. This is something
agnostic enough that is seen on other vendors such as Atmel's SAM line
and others.

A use case for this would be time stamping a rising and/or falling edge
where precision and lack of jitter is important. The only way to currently
do this in zephyr is to set up a GPIO interrupt and then read the counter
or kernel time... but this can have limitations of software such as the
processor may have a lot going on and can be subject to interrupt latencies.
Having a hardware 'latch' done of the rising and/or falling edge with
respect to a timer can eliminate these imprecisions.

How this is to be used, is that an application is to call
`capture_callback_set` with the configuration of the channel number, flags
(such as falling, rising, or both edges), and then a callback function. Then
the `capture_enable` function is to be called to enable this. The callback
has the timestamp of the edge in ticks and the edge that it captured (rising
or falling).

----

~~This also introduces an api for set the counter time.~~

~~Also, this set frequency to be 64 bits rather than 32 bits, as counters, 
such as those that use fractional adders, tick at resolutions
greater than 4294967295Hz. This changes the freq in the common info
to a uint64_t. This retains the existing `counter_get_freq` function which
will still return a 32bit value. This also adds a `counter_get_freq_64`
function to get a 64bit value for the frequency.~~

~~Add inline helper functions for converting ticks to nanoseconds.~~

~~Also implement an inline helper for converting microseconds or
nanoseconds with a 64bit tick value.~~

labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth ISO

BIS termination as broadcaster is handled different than ACL and CIS, and in rare chances the
tx_complete for BIS may not have been completed in the system workqueue before iso_new was called for the same bt_conn struct (e.g. via bt_iso_cig_create), which would perform

k_work_init(&conn->tx_complete_work, tx_complete_work);

but where conn->tx_complete_work still existed in
the system workqueue, which would cause the list
of pending items on the system workqueue to be removed as the `next` pointer would be NULL.

This also adds an assert in bt_conn_new to prevent this issue from appearing again.

title: cmake: refactor `zephyr_get_*_for_lang` functions
body:
**Not for 4.3.**

This PR unifies the implementation of the various `zephyr_get_*_for_lang` functions and their string variants with a generic `zephyr_get_property`, so that the same feature set is available to all wrappers. It also adds several new options that expand the possible use cases:

  - `AS_STRING`: Return the result as a string rather than a list. Equivalent to specifying `DELIMITER " "`.
  - `DELIMITER <delim>`: Specify the output delimiter to use for the list entries. Defaults to `$<SEMICOLON>`.
  - `GENEX`: Use generator expressions to get the property entries at build time, for targets that are not yet fully configured. Cannot be used with `LANG`. Also, CMake will complain if the requested property includes `$<COMPILE_OPTIONS:...>` expressions.
  - `LANG <C|CXX|ASM>`: When set, the property value is filtered for `$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:lang>` entries, and only those matching the given language are kept. Cannot be used with `GENEX`.
  - `PREFIX <prefix>`: Specify a prefix to use for each entry in the output list.
  - `STRIP_PREFIX`: Omit the prefix string, even if given by `PREFIX`.
  - `TARGET <target>`: Specify the target to get the property from. Defaults to `zephyr_interface`.

This work was done while experimenting with alternatives to #98348. It is no longer useful for the EDK, but I think it is still worth considering for merge.

title: twister: Support multiple ports in pytest-twister-harness
body:
This PR adds support for multiple UART connections in `pytest-twister-harness`, enabling testing of multi-core applications where different cores communicate through separate UART interfaces.

Major Refactoring:
* Extracted connection logic from `DeviceAdapter` to new `DeviceConnection` class hierarchy
* Created specialized connection implementations:
  * `SerialConnection` for hardware UART ports
  * `ProcessConnection` for native simulation pipes
  * `FifoConnection` for QEMU FIFO communication

Each connection maintains separate log files (`handler.log` - for backward compatibility, `handler_1.log`, etc.) and can be accessed via `connection_index` parameter in device methods like `readlines_until()` and `write()`.
This enables testing multi-core applications where different cores communicate through separate UART interfaces.

Additional changes:
- Updated unit tests.
- Updated pytest-harness documentation, and docstring in API methods (like `readlines_until()`)
- Updated existing tests that used the `readline_until` method without an explicit `regex` parameter. Since `connection_index` has been added, the `regex` parameter must now be specified explicitly.

-  Updated `sysbuild/hello_world` sample - simplified dual UART testing
- Converted IPC ICMCG  sample from console harness to pytest harness. Added verification of both application and network core output

---
To run samples use:
```
$ZEPHYR_BASE/scripts/twister --no-clean -vv -ll debug \
--west-flash=--erase --device-testing --hardware-map ~/tmp/hardware_map.yml \
-T $ZEPHYR_BASE/samples/subsys/testsuite/pytest/shell \
-s sample.pytest.shell \
-s sample.harness.shell \
-T $ZEPHYR_BASE/samples/sysbuild/hello_world \
-s sample.sysbuild.hello_world.nrf54l15_cpuflpr \
-T $ZEPHYR_BASE/samples/subsys/ipc/ipc_service/icmsg \
-s sample.ipc.icmsg.nrf54l15 \
-s sample.ipc.icmsg.nrf54l15_no_multithreading \
-s sample.ipc.icmsg.nrf54l15_remote_no_multithreading \
-s sample.ipc.icbmsg.nrf54l15 \
-s sample.ipc.icbmsg.nrf54l15_remote_no_multithreading
```
I used nrf54L15DK (instead of hardware map, you can use `-p nrf54l15dk/nrf54l15/cpuapp --device-serial /dev/ttyACM1 --device-serial /dev/ttyACM0` ).
It can also be tested on nrf54H20 or nrf5340dk.
Afer execution, you'll find:
- logs from second core in the console
- a `handler_1.log` file in test output directory

To verify backward compatibility on native / QEMU:
```
$ZEPHYR_BASE/scripts/twister --no-clean  -vv -ll debug \
-p native_sim -p qemu_cortex_m3  \
-T $ZEPHYR_BASE/samples/subsys/testsuite/pytest/shell -s sample.pytest.shell
```

body:
Fix L2CAP configuration negotiation failure when peer device sends MPS value larger than its own TX MTU in the configuration request.

This issue occurs when connecting to certain devices (e.g., iPhone) using enhanced retransmission mode with MAP or PBAP profiles. The peer may send an MPS that exceeds the TX MTU specified in the same L2CAP_CONFIGURATION_REQ packet.

Instead of rejecting the configuration, adjust the MPS to match the peer's TX MTU and include the corrected value in the L2CAP_CONFIGURATION_RSP packet. This allows the connection to proceed while ensuring MPS stays within valid bounds.

title: coap: implement edhoc/oscore support
body:
Let's get edhoc/oscore fully working with standard zephyr samples!

What is the best test suit that we can use in order to verify compliance with all of the RFCs? Shall we perhaps make one based on libcoap client and bats? What do you guys think? 

I have been able to get to the following so far in this branch:

Build coap server with oscore:
```
west build -b qemu_x86 samples/net/coap/coap_server/ -T sample.net.sockets.coap_server.oscore
```

Then start the server. 

Run shell script to test it with default compiled in values:

```
bash samples/net/coap/test-oscore.sh
```

This runs a few requests against the sample server. 

The config for coap client looks like this:
```
# Master Secret (same for client + server)
master_secret,hex,"0102030405060708090a0b0c0d0e0f10"

# Master Salt (optional, but if you use it, must match server)
master_salt,hex,"9e7ca92223786340"

# Sender ID (THIS device, i.e. the client)
sender_id,ascii,"client"

# Recipient ID (remote peer, i.e. the server)
recipient_id,ascii,"server"

# Replay window (usually 32)
replay_window,integer,32

# AEAD algorithm (default is 10 = AES-CCM-16-64-128, but be explicit)
aead_alg,integer,10

# HKDF algorithm (default is -10 = direct+HKDF-SHA-256, optional but can be explicit)
hkdf_alg,integer,-10
```

So far so good.

title: logging: swo: drain hardware pipeline in panic handler
body:
The SWO log backend's `panic()` handler is a no-op. When `LOG_PANIC()`
is called (e.g., before a bootloader jumps to an app, or during a fatal
error), the logging subsystem flushes software buffers to the ITM FIFO,
but the TPIU hardware pipeline still has bytes in-flight on the SWO pin.
The debug probe loses these final messages.

This patch:
1. Spins on `ITM_TCR.BUSY` until the ITM formatter is idle
2. Busy-waits for the TPIU output stage to clock remaining bytes out
   at the configured SWO baud rate

The drain time is estimated from `CONFIG_LOG_BACKEND_SWO_FREQ_HZ`
(~200 bytes × 10 bits/byte with 50% margin). When the frequency is
left at 0 (default = max supported), a conservative 2 ms fallback
is used.

Discovered while working on MCUboot, where SWO logs were lost during
the transition from bootloader to app.

Tested on nRF5340 with J-Link SWO viewer.

title: Bluetooth: Host: Make ACL/CIS disconnect order deterministic
labels: area: Bluetooth;Release Notes;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth ISO
body:
Currently the other of the ACL and CIS disconnect callbacks depend on the order of the HCI events received. Since this order is not specified by the core spec, it means that any users/applications of ISO will need to wait for all CIS disconnects callbacks and the ACL disconnect callback before attempting to reuse any of them.

From an API perspective this is not ideal, and the API will be much simpler if the order of ACL and ISO disconnect callbacks were deterministic, regardless of the controller.

This change postpones the finalization of the ACL disconnect until all the CIS associated with it has been disconnected. This will also make the API more similar to e.g. the L2CAP disconnect order.

No tests have been added since the Zephyr controller always sends the CIS disconnect events first, but other controllers, like the Nordic SDC, may not. See https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/34861 and https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/39514 for the Zephyr implementation. The PR has been manually tested with Nordic SDC to verify the correct behavior.

There will be a follow up PR for LE Audio, as the BAP unicast client has attempted to handle the 2 types of disconnect callbacks in any other, but it is tricky when an ACL `bt_conn` can actually be reused for a new connection, for another device, before the CIS have been properly free'd, since they share some of the same resources in LE Audio.

title: ADC Channel Address Mismatch

body:
### Describe the bug

A change was made in in the ADC API in PR https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/99120 that changed the `ADC_CHANNEL_DT_NODE` behavior.  

Old macro implementation: 
```
 #define ADC_CHANNEL_DT_NODE(ctlr, input) \
     DT_FOREACH_CHILD_VARGS(ctlr, ADC_FOREACH_INPUT, input)
 
 #define ADC_FOREACH_INPUT(node, input) \
     IF_ENABLED(IS_EQ(DT_REG_ADDR_RAW(node), input), (node))
```
In this implementation, the child node's reg property was used in the comparison with input in the macro.  

New macro implementation: 
```
 #define ADC_CHANNEL_DT_NODE(ctlr, input) \
     DT_CHILD_BY_UNIT_ADDR_INT(ctlr, input)
```
In the new implementation, the child node is looked up using the unit address.  

Now for the problem:
In a number of devices, this address is defined as a decimal value when it should be defined as a hex value.  Example from the kit_psc3m5_evk overlay from the adc_dt sample, which results in a reg value of 12, but an address of 18:
```
	channel@12 {
		reg = <12>;
		zephyr,acquisition-time = <ADC_ACQ_TIME_DEFAULT>;
		zephyr,gain = "ADC_GAIN_1";
		zephyr,reference = "ADC_REF_INTERNAL";
		zephyr,resolution = <12>;
	};
```

I can only verify the problem on the Infineon kit_psc3m5_evk board, but I believe the following overlays suffer from the same bug:  
 - `samples/drivers/adc/adc_dt/boards/kit_psc3m5_evk.overlay`

 - `samples/drivers/adc/adc_dt/boards/rzt2m_rsk_r9a07g075m24gbg_cr520.overlay`

title: modbus: rtu: fix buffer overrun in cb_handler_rx
body:
## Summary

`cb_handler_rx()` in `subsys/modbus/modbus_serial.c` uses strict equality (`==`) to check whether `uart_buf[]` is full. If `uart_buf_ctr` ever advances past `CONFIG_MODBUS_BUFFER_SIZE` by even one byte — for any reason — the equality misses forever, `modbus_serial_rx_disable()` is never called again, and every subsequent received byte is written to `*uart_buf_ptr++` at an unbounded offset, silently corrupting adjacent static data.

This PR:

1. Changes the bounds check from `==` to `>=` so the disable still fires on any overshoot, regardless of how the counter got past the buffer size.
2. Loops `uart_fifo_read()` until it returns fewer bytes than requested, per the documented Zephyr UART API contract in `include/zephyr/drivers/uart.h`: *"once uart_irq_rx_ready() is detected, uart_fifo_read() must be called until it reads all available data in the FIFO."*
3. Bails on a negative return from `uart_fifo_read()` (the documented `-ENOSYS` / `-ENOTSUP` cases) without advancing buffer state.

## Field reproducer

Observed on an nRF9151 product reading Modbus RTU over RS485 with an auto-direction transceiver (no DE/RE# pin exposed) that echoes every transmitted byte back into RX. With back-to-back probes and short inter-frame gaps, the RX buffer overflowed before the RTU inter-frame timer fired, the bounds check was bypassed, and `uart_buf_ptr` walked past `uart_buf[]` into the adjacent `timestamp_func` symbol in the logging subsystem's `.data`. The next `LOG_*()` `BLX`'d a garbage address and faulted.

The exact mechanism by which `uart_buf_ctr` overshot 256 on this configuration (`CONFIG_UART_INTERRUPT_DRIVEN=y` with `uart_nrfx_uarte`) is not fully pinned down — `uarte_nrfx_fifo_read()` reads at most one byte per call, so a spec-compliant driver should not advance the counter by more than 1 per IRQ. The `>=` change catches the overshoot regardless of cause and was sufficient to eliminate the field crash; the drain loop separately makes the code conform to the documented API contract.

## Impact

Affects any Zephyr Modbus RTU user where `uart_buf_ctr` can ever cross `CONFIG_MODBUS_BUFFER_SIZE` — most plausibly on auto-direction RS485 transceivers where self-echo makes high-rate fill paths reachable on otherwise idle buses.

## Test plan

- [x] Built on nRF9151; the prior `SECURE_FAULT` is no longer reproducible on the same hardware and Modbus traffic pattern that previously triggered it reliably within minutes.
- [ ] No unit test added — the bug requires an early-missed overrun or a long-running burst that the current Modbus test fixtures do not produce. Open to suggestions on a mock UART driver setup.

Signed-off-by: Diego Solano <diegosolano@gmail.com>

title: STM32MP13 second Ethernet integration
body:
Hello,
This pull request enables the second Ethernet port on the STM32MP135F-DK board.

### Context and Current state

Currently, the ETH_STM32_HAL drivers are singletons and do not support multiple instances. This pull request introduces changes with the following impacts:

- _modules/hal/stm32_ requires modification to support the MP13 in multiple instances.
- _STM32MP135 ETH SRAM memory-region_ must be adapted to provide sufficient space for 2 instances.
- _eth_stm32_hal_* drivers require rework and adaptation.
- STM32MP13 DTSI / DTS must be updated to support 2 Ethernet instances. A new _stm32mp133.dtsi_ file is created as the minimum reference product number supporting two Ethernet controllers.

### Content of the PR

1. **west.yml update**: Update _modules/hal/stm32_ to reference the necessary pull request supporting this feature. When the HAL pull request is merged, remove this west.yml modification.
2. **ETH_SRAM size up**:  Modify the STM32MP135F-DK board to double the Ethernet SRAM size, which is the minimum required for 2 instances.
3. **Zephyr STM32 ETH drivers rework**: Adapt the drivers step by step to prepare for multiple instances.
   * Remove static global declarations of buffers, descriptors, and PHYs, and add them to structures.
   * Remove static unused checks for random MAC address generation, now handled in the Zephyr framework.
   * Switch MP13 REF_CLK configuration from Ethernet controller dedicated to Ethernet controller agnostic.
   * Implement support for multiple instances in the drivers.
4. **DTSI MP13 SoC Support**: Add the new _stm32mp133.dtsi_ file and enable support for the new Ethernet port.
5. **DTS MP135F-DK Board support**: Add the board configuration to enable the second Ethernet port.

### Technical aspects / drivers adaptations

Although the drivers change in many places, the main modifications are:
- Move all static declarations inside eth_stm32_hal_dev_cfg and eth_stm32_hal_dev_data structures to handle one RX buffer, DMA descriptor, or PHY per instance.
- Change eth0* functions to generate them through macros, as done for other multiple instance drivers in Zephyr.

A software choice was made for MCUs supporting only one Ethernet port. As targeted by @arnopo in a previous commit, the HAL differs between STM32MP13, which supports two Ethernet controllers, and other MCUs supporting only one. The STM32MP13 uses the following prototype: _void HAL_ETH_RxAllocateCallback(ETH_HandleTypeDef *heth, uint8_t **buff)_. Other MCUs use: _void HAL_ETH_RxAllocateCallback(uint8_t **buff)_.

@arnopo addressed this by creating the **STM32_ETH_ARGS** macro in _eth_stm32_hal_v2.c_. I completed this by declaring the **ETH_STM32_HAL_CB_HAS_HETH** macro. The approach distinguishes between singleton and multiple instance use cases. In the singleton case, the prototype does not reference a _heth_ pointer, so it redirects to a single instance declared as static. In the multiple instance case, the function uses the _heth_ pointer passed as an argument. This is managed by the **ETH_STM32_HAL_GET_CB_DEVDATA** macro to maintain a consistent implementation.

###  Split ?

If you want to split this pull request into multiple ones, please let me know.

Thanks,
Erwan

title: twister: enable custom reset sequence à la esp32 for other boards
body:
### Summary

I am working with a development board for realtek chips that has a single serial connection and a wiring setup similar to esp32 devboards, where DTR/RTS need to be set to `False` for normal boot.

There is already hard-coded custom serial handling for the `esp32` runner that handles resetting the dev board after flashing via DTR/RTS pins: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/scripts/pylib/twister/twisterlib/handlers.py#L766

Currently, I am using a workaround via `pty_serial` where I do the reset sequence in a custom python script, but the `pty_serial` option is not supported on windows due to it using virtual com ports from pySerial that are mac/unix only.

So I need a "native" solution in twister to set DTR/RTS state to make the board boot successfully after flashing.

### Describe the solution you'd like

While adding additional config for the serial port seems like a quick win, something does not sit right with me  regarding the current approach of wrapping a process in a virtual serial port. That looks like a workaround to begin with.

It seems that an abstraction to communicate with the DUT with two implementations (`serial` and `process`) would be a cleaner approach that would fix the incompatibility with windows and allows to keep all of the flexibility that `serial_pty` offers over just being able to configure the serial parameters.

### Alternatives

While the proposed refactor solves the problem for now, requiring a full-blown python script that does input and output redirection just to set some serial parameters seems like it does not solve the problem fully.

So it would probably still be helpful to be able to control more serial port options via the config.

### Additional Context

`serial_pty` "script" I am using: `rtkprog terminal` -> https://github.com/a-labs-io/rtkprog/blob/c74034576337ae4b51fe06b8068831cb452f1d18/rtkprog/cli.py#L121

title: modem: pipe: support dual transmit buffers
body:
Rework of #98541 to address compatibility feedback.
The existing function `modem_pipe_transmit` continues to work as it does now, regardless of backend support for `transmit_double`.
The new function `modem_pipe_transmit_double` works regardless of backend support for `transmit_double`.

Handle sending the request and delimiter strings in a single call to the pipe backend. This has two advantages:
     1. No time gap between request and delimiter on the interface (more efficient line utilization)
     2. Fewer bytes transmitted on the line for pipes that perform wrapping (CMUX).

For example, sending "ATE0" + "\n" through CMUX now takes 11 bytes, instead of the previous 17 bytes (10 + 7):
```
[00:00:38.268,064] <wrn> modem_cmux: TX
                                     f9 0b ef 0b 41 54 45 30  0d 5d f9                |....ATE0 .].
```

The double buffer send functionality is exposed through a new function in the modem pipe API, meaning all existing code does not require any changes.

title: Add a ZMS iterator API to enumerate live entries without a predefined ID list
labels: area: Samples;area: Tests;area: Storage;area: Key-Value Storage Systems
body:
This PR  introduces the iterator API, adds mask-based filtering support at initialization,
and then adds the related tests, sample usage, and documentation.

## Why

Applications that do not maintain a separate ID index need a way to discover
currently live entries directly from ZMS. The iterator API provides that
capability, and optional masking allows narrowing enumeration to relevant IDs.

## Behavior

When using zms_iter_next:
   - Iterator returns live entries only
   - Header entries are skipped
   - Deleted entries are skipped
   - Older revisions are skipped (latest live entry is returned)

When using zms_iter_next_all:
   - Iterator returns all entries (even old entries)
   - Deleted entries are returned as well
   - Header entries are skipped

Default initialization enumerates all live IDs
Masked initialization enumerates only IDs matching the provided mask

title: Bluetooth: Controller: nRF54L: Add dual-timer support
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Samples;platform: nRF;area: Tests;Stale;area: Bluetooth Controller;area: Bluetooth Host;platform: nRF BSIM
body:
Add support for using NRF_TIMER00 in the MCU power domain as the EVENT_TIMER for event timing, while keeping NRF_TIMER10 in the Radio power domain as the SW_SWITCH_TIMER for tIFS switch timings.

This is enabled when CONFIG_BT_CTLR_SW_SWITCH_SINGLE_TIMER=n on SOC_COMPATIBLE_NRF54LX. The default remains single-timer (TIMER10 for both), preserving backward compatibility.

Cross-domain DPPI connections use three PPIB bridges:
  PPIB11/PPIB21: Radio <-> Peripheral (GRTC -> NRF_TIMER10, existing)
  PPIB00/PPIB10: MCU <-> Radio (NRF_TIMER00 <-> Radio peripherals)
  PPIB01/PPIB20: MCU <-> Peripheral (GRTC -> NRF_TIMER00, new)

DPPIC00 channels 0-5 are assigned for the six EVENT_TIMER connections:
  ch 0: GRTC -> NRF_TIMER00 START (via PPIB20/PPIB01)
  ch 1: NRF_TIMER00 COMPARE -> Radio TXEN/RXEN (via PPIB00/PPIB10)
  ch 2: Radio READY -> NRF_TIMER00 CAPTURE (via PPIB10/PPIB00)
  ch 3: Radio ADDRESS -> NRF_TIMER00 CAPTURE (via PPIB10/PPIB00)
  ch 4: NRF_TIMER00 COMPARE -> Radio DISABLE (via PPIB00/PPIB10)
  ch 5: Radio END -> NRF_TIMER00 CAPTURE (via PPIB10/PPIB00)

Timer prescaler values:
  NRF_TIMER00 (HFPLL 128 MHz): prescaler 7 -> 1 MHz resolution
  NRF_TIMER10 (HFXO 32 MHz):  prescaler 5 -> 1 MHz resolution

DPPIC00 and PPIB bridge channel reservations are declared in bt_ctlr_used_resources.h and mapped to nrfx resource tracking in nrfx_reserved_resources.h.

Requires CONFIG_BT_CTLR_NRF_GRTC (default y on nRF54L) since the PPIB01/PPIB20 bridge for GRTC -> NRF_TIMER00 is only configured in the GRTC event path.

title: Bluetooth: HIDS: add HID Service
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Samples;area: Tests;area: Bluetooth Host;platform: nRF BSIM;area: MAINTAINER File;Release
body:
## Summary

Adds the HID Service (HIDS), the GATT service the HID Device role of HOGP is built on, a `hids` Bluetooth shell command set, and a two device bsim test.

Follows the Bluetooth WG decision in https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/109578#issuecomment-5526424590: HIDS lands as a standalone service under `services/hids/`, the HOGP Device wrapper that only forwarded to it is dropped, and `profiles/` is left to the HOGP Host role, which is a real profile rather than a stub. So there is no `profiles/` directory and no `bt_hogp_device_*` API here.

Phase 1 of RFC #108582.

## Commits

1. `Bluetooth: HIDS: add HID Service` — the service and the `bt_hids_*` API
2. `Bluetooth: HIDS: add HID Service shell commands` — `CONFIG_BT_HIDS_SHELL`
3. `tests: Bluetooth: HIDS: add a two device bsim test`

Each commit builds and passes its tests on its own.

## Design notes

* **The attribute table is static.** How many Report characteristics of each type exist is Kconfig; the application supplies one Report ID per characteristic at registration. Building it at runtime would mean either exposing Reports the application does not use, or putting a CCC on Output and Feature Reports, which HIDS does not define.
* **The service holds each Report value** and answers a Host read from it, like the other GATT services in the tree. Every fragment of a long read comes from that one value rather than from a per-read copy that can go stale. The application uses `bt_hids_report_set()` and `bt_hids_report_get()`; a Host write to a writable Report replaces the value too.
* This replaces an earlier `get_report` callback per read. ATT does not read a long attribute atomically, so a per-read callback cannot stay consistent without a cache whose lifetime ATT gives no way to bound. Two consequences: memory becomes one buffer per Report instead of per connection (336 to 1096 bytes of static data with 1/1/2 Reports at `MAX_REPORT_LEN=256`), and the application is no longer told that a Host did GET_REPORT.
* **Protocol Mode and Suspend are per connection**, held in a slot from a pool of `MIN(CONFIG_BT_MAX_CONN, CONFIG_BT_MAX_PAIRED)` slots, claimed when a Host's link is encrypted or on its first Protocol Mode or HID Control Point access, and reset on every connection. A Host that finds the pool full when it encrypts is simply not tracked. CCC changes are reported with the connection they belong to.
* **Writes are bounded.** Longer than `CONFIG_BT_HIDS_MAX_REPORT_LEN` gets Invalid Attribute Length, so that option bounds both directions; a non-zero offset gets Invalid Offset, because a Report is a whole report rather than a byte addressable blob.
* **Checked at registration:** Report Map length, duplicate Report IDs within a Report Type, a Report ID of 0 when a type has several Reports, and HID Information flags the service cannot back.
* **Protocol Mode is off by default** and selected by the two Boot Report options, because the characteristic is mandatory only for a Device that supports Boot Protocol Mode.
* **Boot Reports** take their layout from the USB HID Specification rather than the Report Map, so they have no Report Reference descriptor, and only the two Boot Input Reports have a CCC. Keyboard and mouse get separate options because HIDS v1.1 Table 2.1 allows each only on that device type. Staying inside the selected Protocol Mode is the Host's requirement, so neither set is restricted; the application picks what to send from `bt_hids_get_protocol_mode()`.
* **Not implemented:** multiple HID Service instances, the External Report Reference descriptor, HID ISO.

## Test plan

* **bsim, two devices** (`tests/bsim/bluetooth/services/hids`): the client encrypts the link, discovers the service, checks the Report Map, the HID Information and every Report Reference descriptor, subscribes, then exercises GET_REPORT, SET_REPORT, Protocol Mode and the HID Control Point. It reconnects and checks that Protocol Mode is back at its default and notifications resume, that unregistering does not disconnect the Host, and that registering again while that Host is connected tracks it.
* Also in bsim: the three Boot Report characteristics (properties, which of them have a CCC, each fixed length, a Boot Keyboard Input notification, and a wrong length write refused before the application sees it); the registration checks; the bound `bt_hids_send_report()` enforces; a CCC write asking for indications refused while a Reserved bit is processed as zero; a Read Long, and a Read Blob at and past the end of the value.
* **Build matrix**, warnings as errors: `BT_HIDS` alone, with the shell at 1/1/1, `PROTOCOL_MODE=y`, each Boot option alone and both together, 16/16/16 with the shell off at `MAX_REPORT_LEN=256`, and 1/0/0 with the shell off. All three counts at 0 fails a `BUILD_ASSERT`, as intended.
* **Hardware, two USB dongles** over HCI User Channel, Zephyr on both sides (Realtek 5.4 as the Device, CSR 4.2 as the Host): the attribute table as designed; bonding, discovery, GET_REPORT, SET_REPORT, notifications, Protocol Mode and HID Control Point all reaching the application; a 100-byte Report over a 66-byte ATT MTU assembled from two Read Blobs, with one past the end answered Invalid Offset; a 20-byte and a queued 64-byte write against an 8-byte `MAX_REPORT_LEN` both refused with ATT `0x0d` without reaching the application, and a write within the limit delivered.
* `checkpatch.pl` and `check_compliance.py` are clean on each commit.
* CI does not run the bsim suite for this PR — `BabbleSim Test Results` reports no tests — so the bsim result above is local, on `nrf52_bsim/native`.
* PTS has not been re-run since the restructuring; the 20/20 result posted earlier in this PR was obtained on the original single-commit version and no longer applies.

## Follow-ups

* `peripheral_hogp` sample, stacked on this branch: #118458. It also removes `samples/bluetooth/peripheral_hids`, whose Report Map is readable on an unencrypted link, which HOGP does not allow.
* HOGP Host role, which is where `profiles/` gets introduced: #109579.

title: soc: rp2350: Support basic AMP with Snippets
labels: area: Build System;area: Samples;area: IPC;area: Devicetree;area: Tests;area: Clock Control;area: Devicetree Binding;area: PM CPU ops;platform: Raspberry Pi Pico;area: mbox;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
Continuation of #93379. Creating a new PR because cherry-picked commits needed to be squashed with some changes. Thanks to @dsseng for the support!

Add support to launch the 2nd core (CPU1) of the rp2350 from the main core (CPU0) for the Cortex-M33 CPUs using the new `rp2xxx-cpu1` and `rp2xxx-cpu1-xip` snippets (naming suggestions appreciated). The `rp2xxx-cpu1[-xip]` snippets are modeled after the [`nordic-flpr`](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/snippets/nordic/nordic-flpr/README.html#).

Add support to launch the 2nd core (CPU1) of the rp2350 from the main core (CPU0) for the Cortex-M33 CPUs.

Add the rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33/cpu1 board target that is has 256kB SRAM, gpio controller, and uart1 by default. CPU0 is responsible for launching CPU1 in a soc late init hook. When CPU0's board dts has `&cpu1`'s node with an `enable-method = "raspberrypi,pico-pcbs";` and a `cpu_enable` node with a matching compatible.

The `raspberrypi,pico-pcbs` node provides `source-memory` and `execution-memory` properties to the CPU0 board target.  

If CPU0's board dts has both `source-memory` and `execution-memory` properties in `cpu1-launcher`, CPU0 will copy CPU1's image from `source-memory` into `execution-memory` and assumes that CPU1's CONFIG_XIP=n (the default). If only `execution-memory` is present, it is assumed that CPU1's CONFIG_XIP=y. This is modeled after a combination of the [Analog Devices max78002evkit](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/adi/max78002evkit/doc/index.html) and Nordic's [vpr launcher driver](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/drivers/misc/nordic_vpr_launcher/nordic_vpr_launcher.c).

**Note:** Running both CPU0 and CPU1 XIP is much slower than running CPU1 from SRAM because of XIP cache contention between the 2 cores. However, it may be necessary if CPU1's image does not fit in SRAM.

Although CPU1 is a board variant, this PR does not yet support using it as an independent target like the `cpuflpr`. This would require some custom sysbuild.cmake magic as seen [here](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/soc/nordic/sysbuild.cmake).

---

Open Questions:
- Is it ok to have a board variant that can't be built on its own yet and leave that to some future work?
- Right now, we would have to make a `rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33/cpu1/mcuboot` target to support the mcuboot board target. This is the same for other boards that has a different flash size/partition layout. This looks like we will have to have a partitioning scheme similar to [how espressif does it](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/tree/main/dts/vendor/espressif).  Is that required for this PR to be merged?
- The [board porting guide recommendations](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/hardware/porting/board_porting.html#general-recommendations) says that a board should have a `zephyr,console` chosen node. Is that still required for the CPU1 board target if it's always a secondary core? I enabled &uart1, but there was previous conversation that adding the `uart1_default` pinctrl to the common pinctrl file is not acceptable. (see https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/93379#discussion_r2286093435). Is it ok in the cpu1 common dtsi?

Future work: 
- Support hazard3 rp2350 core launch CPU1: need to use an architecture agnostic `WFE` and `SEV` in CPU1 launch sequence and to set CPU1's architecture to the Hazard3 core.
- Verify AMP on more rp2350-based boards
- Support RP2040
- Support using CPU1 as independent target like `cpuflpr` if there is desire for it.

---

Testing:

Build the icmsg sample with: 

```
west build -p always -b rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33 --sysbuild -S rp2xxx-cpu1 samples/subsys/ipc/ipc_service/icmsg/
# or for CPU1 with XIP: 
west build -p always -b rpi_pico2/rp2350a/m33 --sysbuild -S rp2xxx-cpu1-xip samples/subsys/ipc/ipc_service/icmsg/
```

Flash with west using the RaspberryPi OpenOCD fork according to [Programming and Debugging](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/boards/raspberrypi/rpi_pico/doc/index.html#programming-and-debugging) section of rpi_pico's board docs.

```
west flash --openocd /usr/local/bin/openocd
```

title: drivers: spi: nrfx_spim: chunk transfers exceeding EasyDMA MAXCNT
body:
The reworked SPIM driver passes the whole continuous chunk returned by spi_context_max_continuous_chunk() straight to the common transfer layer, which rejects anything larger than the controller MAXCNT with -EINVAL. On SoCs with a small EasyDMA MAXCNT (e.g. nRF91 SPIM with 13 bits, max 8191 bytes) a transfer of 8192 bytes or more fails outright.

The old monolithic driver used to cap the chunk to the MAXCNT limit and let the event handler walk the rest of the buffer. That behaviour was lost in the rework, so any caller pushing a buffer larger than MAXCNT now breaks. One example is the nRF70 firmware patch download, which copies the patch in 8192 byte chunks and ends up corrupting RPU memory, leading to a boot signature mismatch.

Restore the cap in transfer_start() so an oversized chunk is split across multiple EasyDMA transfers, with the remainder handled by the next call from the event handler once the current chunk completes.

title: gpio: RFC: Add Fast GPIO API Extension (closes #106831)
labels: area: GPIO;area: Devicetree;platform: STM32;platform: nRF;platform: NXP;area: Tests;platform: Microchip SAM;platform: ESP32;area: Devicetree Binding;platform: Raspberry Pi Pico;area: MAINTAINER File;Release
body: This commit creates the Fast GPIO API via RFC #106831. It adds low-latency set, clear, toggle, get, etc. functions and helpers for implementing fast bit-bang drivers. Closes #11917, closes #106831. **UPDATE:** This has been refactored to use DT instead of overrides; see more recent commits. ~~**NOTE:** This is starting as a draft. I want to get some feedback from @nandojve before opening to other reviewers. Before marking as ready I will separate the WS2812 driver parts into a new PR. It is combined here at first for ease of testing/hardware verification.~~ This is now complete: #111218. OK, this was a tough one! Here are some notes compared to the original RFC: 1. I was unable to implement `gpio_fast_send_stream()`. The timing requirements for a driver like WS2812 are too tight to abstract the data out into a struct and for loops. I was only able to make it work by creating a specific 2-operations-per-bit set/clear mode, which defeats the point of the abstraction. It is likely possible, but will take a lot more work and I think should go in a followup PR. 2. The only way I could make the timings reliable across all platforms was to use `nop`. 3. I could not use `LISTIFY()` because it created a mess of Kconfig math. We can now automatically calculate timing offsets via the number of CPU cycles required for set and clear in the header/source, so the WS2812 driver no longer requires per-board timing config in Kconfig/DTS. 4. When implementing future vendor Fast GPIO drivers, it is really a **requirement** that it is tested on real hardware. There are so many edge cases where you may need `__ramfunc` or calculating the cycle offsets are weird. The good thing is, **none of these edge cases are visible from the user-facing API.** 5. The number of cycles to do operations varies per platform, but **the driver can fully realize if timings can be met at compile time.** The part I am really proud of: I have verified this works on **6 different platforms!** - Adafruit Circuit Playground Express: `sam0` - Adafruit Feather ESP32: `esp32` - Adafruit KB2040: `rpi_pico` - Teensy 4.0: `mcux` - STM32 Nucleo-F401RE: `stm32` - nRF52840 Dongle : `nrf52840` All of these work without custom timing in DTS. @nandojve I added your copyright to some files since you did a lot of work in the RFC. Please let me know if you would prefer me to remove them. I used the help of Claude Opus 4.7 on this PR, and it mostly helped me with vendor-specifics for each platform that I am less familiar with. I have physically tested the set/clear functions on each platform. I do not use this tool for issue/PR comments and take full responsibility for this code. Assisted-by: Claude:claude-opus-4.7

title: subsys: debug: fix mipi stp unaligned access with clang

The fast nibble-copy path in the MIPI STP decoder assumes unaligned
multiword accesses are safe on Cortex-M.

With clang on mps2/an385 this can still generate unaligned accesses in
the optimized path, causing a UsageFault in debug.mipi_stp_decoder.

Disable the fast path for clang (and when unaligned trapping is enabled),
falling back to the existing byte-wise safe path.

title: net: l2: ethernet: validate MAC after driver start
body:
net: l2: ethernet: validate MAC after driver start
    
  Commit 481035cf8e1 ("net: ethernet: check mac address when bringing a
  eth iface up") validated the link address before eth->start() was
  called. That broke Wi-Fi interfaces whose MAC is learnt from firmware
  during bring-up (e.g. nRF70 reads it from OTP once the companion
  firmware boots), leaving them unable to admin-up and preventing WPA
  supplicant from registering them. The offending commit was reverted in
  d8065e9f87c to unblock nRF Wi-Fi.
  
  Reintroduce the validation, but run eth->start() first so that drivers
  which populate their address during bring-up have a valid link address
  by the time it is checked. This keeps the useful diagnostic for
  misconfigured MACs while supporting drivers that only know their
  address after start.
  
  A failure of the post-start validation is terminal: net_if_up() fails
  and the interface is left unusable, the same as if eth->start() itself
  had failed. Return -EINVAL directly rather than rolling back with
  eth->stop(), so the behaviour is consistent for drivers that do not
  implement a stop op.
  
  Signed-off-by: Chaitanya Tata <Chaitanya.Tata@nordicsemi.no>

title: soc: infineon: edge: pse84: scope MPU regions to owning core
body:
The PSE84 static MPU region table is shared between the Cortex-M33 and
Cortex-M55 cores, but several of the regions only belong to one core.
Instantiating every region on both cores wastes scarce hardware MPU
slots. On a core with few data regions this leaves no room for
memory-domain partitions: the default domain can no longer allocate its
libc/malloc partitions and initialization fails with `-ENOSPC`
(`Failed to add default memory partition (-28)` /
`no free partition slots available`), which traps the kernel at boot and
breaks the userspace / memory-protection tests.

This scopes each single-core region to the core that actually owns it.

### Changes

- **`m55_allocatable_shared`** — a CM55-only nocache window; unused on
  the CM33. Now gated to `CONFIG_CPU_CORTEX_M55`.
- **`m33s_code` / `m33_code`** — hold the CM33 secure / non-secure code
  images; the CM55 never executes from them. `m33_code` is additionally
  only meaningful for a non-secure CM33 image (it is empty on the secure
  CM33 build), so it is gated off there too. Now gated to
  `!CONFIG_CPU_CORTEX_M55` (and, for `m33_code`,
  `CONFIG_CPU_CORTEX_M33 && !CONFIG_TRUSTED_EXECUTION_SECURE`).
- **`itcm` / `dtcm`** — the CM55 tightly-coupled memories; the CM33 cores
  never access them. Now gated to `CONFIG_CPU_CORTEX_M55`.
- **`m33_allocatable_shared`** is intentionally left on both cores, since
  it backs shared-memory consumers and is not specific to a single core.

On the secure CM33 build this reduces the static set to
`{FLASH, SRAM, SHARED_MEMORY_33, M33S_CODE}` (4 regions), restoring the
partition slots the default memory domain needs.

### Testing

- **CM55** (`kit_pse84_ai/pse846gps2dbzc4a/m55`, sysbuild,
  `tests/kernel/mem_protect/userspace`): before — boot trap,
  `no free partition slots available`, no tests run; after — full suite
  passes (`userspace` 32/0/2, `userspace_domain` 4/0/0,
  `userspace_domain_ctx` 3/0/0, `PROJECT EXECUTION SUCCESSFUL`).
- **CM33**: verified the static region table is reduced to 4 entries
  (`mpu_config.num_regions == 4`), so the default memory domain regains
  its partition budget.

labels: area: UART;area: Devicetree;platform: STM32;platform: nRF;platform: NXP;platform: Microchip SAM;platform: ESP32;area: Devicetree Binding;Stale
body:
This PR adds property `framing-error-reporting` to UART drivers. This property allows a driver to expect how to actively handle a framing error if the next byte after a framing error needs to be read (for protocols like DMX512).

I am working on a DMX driver for Zephyr. DMX signals the start of a packet with a "Mark After Break" signal, which is interpreted as a framing error or break error on a UART. The next byte after the error is valid data that is a part of the packet. Normally, a line error would probably mean throwing away the data immediately before and after, but here I need to keep the data following the error. I have this working with Zephyr APIs on a bunch of platforms, but it is impossible for the driver to handle UART error handling type without knowing at compile time/runtime.

title: tracing: Configurable init level
body:
The tracing backend initialized at a fixed `APPLICATION` level. Make the `SYS_INIT` level (`TRACING_INIT_LEVEL`) and priority (`TRACING_INIT_PRIORITY`) configurable so tracing can come up earlier and capture more of the boot sequence.

The earliest level is `PRE_KERNEL_2` (sync tracing only — async needs the kernel for its drainer thread), and it requires a priority above the system timer (`SYSTEM_CLOCK_INIT_PRIORITY`) so the cycle counter is live and event timestamps are valid. The defaults (`APPLICATION`, priority 0) preserve the previous behavior.

The kernel already calls `sys_trace_sys_init_enter/exit` around every `SYS_INIT` and device init, but the CTF backend stubbed them out. Implement them so per-init timing is captured.

Record the device name when the entry is a device, so the event is self-describing in any CTF reader. Bare `SYS_INIT` entries have no runtime name, so the `init_fn` pointer is recorded instead for offline resolution. The init level and result are included as well.

title: drivers: timer: add NXP RTC (rtc_jdp) system timer
labels: area: Kernel;area: Counter;area: Timer;platform: NXP;area: Tests;platform: NXP MCU;area: Boards/SoCs
body:
## Summary

Add a Zephyr system timer driver for the NXP RTC (`rtc_jdp`) IP on the MCXE31x family, letting the RTC serve as the kernel tick source. Because the RTC keeps counting across all low-power states, it works as a low-power system timer with no companion timer. The RTC counter driver already exists; this PR adds the system-timer role on the same IP plus the arbitration so the two roles coexist.

## Design

It is a chosen-selected singleton (enabled via `zephyr,system-timer` -> an `nxp,rtc-jdp` node, like `mcux_lptmr_timer.c`), tickless against the RTC's single absolute compare register (RTCVAL), with the free-running 32-bit counter as the cycle counter. A RTCVAL write synchronizes into the slow RTC clock domain and sets `INV_RTC` while in progress (further writes are ignored), so the driver waits for `INV_RTC` to clear before each write per the reference manual. The scheduling horizon is capped at half the counter range so an absolute compare can never wrap past the counter and look like the past (mirroring `mcux_os_timer.c`/`mcux_gpt_timer.c`). The MCXE31x defconfig disables SysTick and derives the clock rate from the chosen node when this timer is selected (prescaler = 1 -> 32 kHz, 1000 ticks/s). The counter driver yields the RTC instance when it is the chosen system timer so both drivers never bind the same hardware. The role is opt-in; the board default (SysTick + RTC-counter calendar) is unchanged.

## Testing

Validated on `frdm_mcxe31b`: `tests/kernel/timer/timer_api` passes 15/15, and `tests/kernel/timer/timer_behavior` passes with zero drift and zero jitter over 10,000 samples (mean exactly 32 cycles/tick, `late_callbacks = 0`). Default-build regressions confirm SysTick stays the default and the RTC counter still instantiates when the RTC is not the system timer.

title: net: lib: coap: client: Wake poll() when a request is scheduled
body:
`coap_client_schedule_poll()` only gives the `recv` semaphore, which wakes the `recv` thread when it is idle but does not interrupt a `poll()` that is already blocked. A request submitted mid-poll - in particular one whose socket changed after a reconnect - is then not watched until the current `poll()` returns, up to `COAP_PERIODIC_TIMEOUT` later, so its response is invisible for that window.

Write the recv-thread wakeup `eventfd` from `schedule_poll()` so a blocked `poll()` returns at once and the `recv` loop rebuilds `fds[]` with the current socket set. The `eventfd` is the same channel cancellation already uses; the resulting ack-sem pulse is harmless since the cancel path resets it under the cancel mutex before waiting. Update the eventfd documentation to cover the dual use.

title: bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state validation in receive path
labels: area: Bluetooth;area: Bluetooth Host;area: Bluetooth Classic;backport v3.7-branch;backport v4.3-branch;backport v4.4-branch
body:
* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state transition for fixed channel

Add proper state management to Bluetooth Classic L2CAP fixed channel connection by setting the channel state to `CONNECTED` before invoking the connected callback.

The change ensures that fixed channels follow the same state transition pattern as other L2CAP channel types. When a fixed channel is connected, the state is now explicitly set to `BT_L2CAP_CONNECTED` before calling the channel's connected callback.

The changes ensure the channel state accurately reflects its lifecycle status.

* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: use chan state to manage fixed channel

Refactor the fixed channel accept functions to use channel state for direct check if the channel is available instead of checking `conn` field of channel. And also refactor the fixed channel accept functions to use connection index for direct lookup instead of iterating through the pool arrays.

The changes affect the L2CAP BR signaling channel, connectionless channel, and SMP BR channel accept functions.

The functions now check if the channel is in the `DISCONNECTED` state before accepting a new connection, returning `-EBUSY` if the channel is not idle. This ensures proper channel state validation and prevents reuse of channels that are still in use.

Additionally, instead of searching through the entire pool to find an available channel context, the code now uses `bt_conn_index()` to directly access the corresponding entry in the pool array.

The L2CAP BR fixed channel connection now also sets the channel state to CONNECTING, ensuring proper state transitions.

* bluetooth: classic: l2cap: add state validation in receive path

Add state validation check in the L2CAP BR/EDR receive path to ensure channels are in a valid connected state before processing incoming data.

The change adds a check after the fixed channel validation to verify that the channel state is at least BT_L2CAP_CONNECTED before proceeding with data reception. If the channel is in an earlier state (CONNECTING or DISCONNECTED), an error is logged and the packet is dropped.

This prevents potential issues from processing data on channels that are not yet fully established or are in the process of being torn down, improving the robustness of the L2CAP receive path.

Fixes: #113698

title: drivers: pcie: host: add configuration space write utility to shell
body:
## Subsystem: Drivers / PCIe Host

### Problem Statement & Architectural Context
The current PCIe host shell module implementation (`drivers/pcie/host/shell.c`) is entirely passive. While it permits early boot device discovery, configuration dump reading, and capability tree parsing via `pcie ls`, it lacks an interactive mechanism to perform real-time, runtime configuration updates or write instrumentations from the command canvas.

This presents a development bottleneck during pre-silicon platform validation (e.g., when debugging complex ARM-FPGA SoC interconnects such as Intel/Altera or AMD/Xilinx AXI-to-PCIe bridges) where engineers need to rapidly toggle interface control registers, force-enable bus-master states, or dynamically alter memory maps without modifying code and repeatedly recompiling the firmware image target.

### Proposed Feature Enhancements
This patch introduces a runtime interactive sub-command wrapper: 
`pcie write <bus:device.function> <register_word_offset> <32bit_hex_data>`

**Underlying Execution Steps:**
1. Intercepts terminal panel strings, isolating target registers and data components.
2. Checks configuration space link responsiveness to prevent system lockups.
3. Invokes the underlying hardware abstraction layer function `pcie_conf_write()` natively over the specified index.
4. Executes an immediate configuration read-back loop pass to verify bit-latch and alignment stability.

### Verification Matrix
- **Compilation Toolsuite:** Zephyr SDK 1.0.1 (`aarch64-zephyr-elf-gcc`)
- **Validation Architecture:** Out-of-tree workspace layout running on top of a 64-bit multi-core simulator (`qemu_cortex_a53`).
- **Code Standards Compliance:** Evaluated cleanly via `checkpatch.pl` linting scripts, logging `0 errors, 0 warnings, 446 lines checked`.
- **Live Functional Logs:** Successfully toggled the Bus Master Enable (BME) and Memory Space Enable (MSE) bits inside the Command/Status register from `0x00000000` to `0x00000006` dynamically with real-time verification feedback.

title: drivers: display: ssd16xx: add support for SSD1683
body:
The Solomon Systech **SSD1683** is a Gen2 SSD16xx EPD controller (functionally
equivalent to the SSD1619A, **400 sources × 300 gates**). It uses the same
command set as the already-supported SSD1680/SSD1681 and loads its refresh
waveforms from OTP, so support is just a new devicetree binding plus a
`ssd16xx_quirks` entry with the correct maximum resolution — no custom LUT.

Used by e.g. the **WeAct Studio 4.2" 400×300** module and the GoodDisplay
**GDEY042T81** 4.2" 400×300 mono panel.

Per the driver's own convention (`struct ssd16xx_quirks`: `max_width` = gate
lines, `max_height` = source outputs; cross-checked against SSD1680 =
176 sources × 296 gates → `max_width=296, max_height=176`), SSD1683
(300 gates, 400 sources) → `max_width=300, max_height=400`.

## Changes
- `drivers/display/ssd16xx.c`: add `quirks_solomon_ssd1683` + registration.
- `dts/bindings/display/solomon,ssd1683.yaml`: new binding (includes
  `solomon,ssd16xx-common.yaml`, mirrors the existing `solomon,ssd1680.yaml`).

## Test overlay used
```dts
&spi0 {
    status = "okay";
    cs-gpios = <&gpio0 0 GPIO_ACTIVE_LOW>;

    epd: ssd1683@0 {
        compatible = "solomon,ssd1683";
        reg = <0>;
        mipi-max-frequency = <4000000>;
        width  = <296>;   /* gates; see note below on the /8 constraint */
        height = <400>;   /* sources, multiple of 8 */
        busy-gpios = <&gpio0 1 GPIO_ACTIVE_HIGH>;
        full { };         /* empty -> OTP waveform */
    };
};
```

## Tested on hardware
Verified on a **Nordic nRF52840 (pro micro dev board)** driving a **WeAct Studio 4.2" 400×300**
e-paper module (SSD1683 controller) over SPI, via LVGL. Both **full and partial
refresh** render correctly in both orientations:
- **Landscape** — native geometry (the byte-packed axis is the 400-source side,
  which is a multiple of 8).
- **Portrait** — with `width = 296` (a /8-safe value ≤ 300 gates), matching the
  workaround for the LVGL-glue limitation described below.

## Known limitation
A GDEY042T81 has 300 gates, and 300 is **not a multiple of 8**. Zephyr's LVGL
mono glue (`modules/lvgl/lvgl_display_mono.c`) mis-strides 1-bit buffers whose
width is not a multiple of 8. That is an **LVGL-glue issue, not an ssd16xx
issue**, so this PR is deliberately limited to enabling the controller. Use
`width = 296` (a /8 value ≤ 300 gates) or landscape orientation (the 400-source
axis is /8). A proper stride fix belongs in a separate LVGL-glue PR.

## Checks run locally
- `checkpatch.pl`: 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `yamllint` (Zephyr config): clean
- devicetree binding schema (edtlib): parses, compatible matches filename,
  include resolves (46 inherited props), no underscore/`required:false` issues
- `gitlint` (Zephyr config): clean
- DCO: author == Signed-off-by (`Marcus Voß <meav33@gmail.com>`)

labels: area: Kernel;area: Tests;area: MAINTAINER File;area: Boards/SoCs;platform: Realtek Bee
body:
1. Remove hardcoded TIMESLICE_SIZE default (rtl87x2g, rtl8752h)

  The SoC-level default of 10 ms caused tracing samples (sample.tracing.user, sample.tracing.gpio) to stall at 115200 baud: three consecutive trace hooks after each sys-timer ISR emit ~9–12 ms of synchronous UART output, exhausting the timeslice before application threads get CPU time. Removing the override lets the kernel default (20 ms) apply, which provides sufficient headroom.

**### Delete these two related commits for root cause solve PR:** 
  2. Tune zephyr,min-timeout-cycles to 30 (rtl87x2g, rtl8752h) ->https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113083

  With MIN_DELAY = 32 = CYC_PER_TICK, the per-ISR overhead from elapsed() and drift correction accumulates without bound until the unannounced surplus reaches 2 * CYC_PER_TICK, triggering dticks=2 and firing two k_timer callbacks back-to-back in a single ISR. This appears as a ~1-cycle (31 µs) spurious period in tests/kernel/timer/timer_behavior. Setting MIN_DELAY = 30 (drain rate = 2 cycles/tick) resolves the accumulation. The value was validated by test on both platforms.

  3. Relax IDLE_EVENT_STATS_PRECISION for 32 kHz SysTick platforms  ->  https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113075

The default 1% precision in tests/kernel/usage/thread_runtime_stats is unachievable at 32 kHz: with peak_cycles ~ 32, a single cycle deviation already represents ~3%. Raised to 7% for SOC_SERIES_RTL87X2G and SOC_SERIES_RTL8752H, consistent with the existing relaxation for RISC-V targets.

It addresses the issue mentioned in #107533 PR. The direction the PR was taking would take more time to converge than opening another one.  

Please @MarkoSagadin, review this one and check if it solves what you were meant to solve.

title: drivers: gpio: gpio_mcux: support GPIO_DISCONNECTED in PORT variant
body:
The PORT-based gpio_mcux_port_configure() rejects any configuration that sets neither GPIO_INPUT nor GPIO_OUTPUT with -ENOTSUP. This makes it impossible to release a pin with gpio_pin_configure(dev, pin, GPIO_DISCONNECTED), which applications such as debug probes and programmers need in order to tri-state shared target pins (SWD, ICSP, UPDI) when a protocol is deactivated.

Handle GPIO_DISCONNECTED by clearing the pin's direction bit in PDDR, turning it into an input. Since no pull flags are present in a disconnect request, the pull resistors are also disabled by the existing PCR logic below, leaving the pin floating (high impedance).

Tested by building samples/subsys/dap for frdm_mcxa156; the change has been shipping as a downstream patch in our probe firmware (MCXA156), where it releases shared programming pins between protocol switches.

title: Bluetooth: Mesh: delayable_msg: fix NULL deref on empty busy list (#113175)
body:
Fixes #113175.

## Problem

`delayable_msg_handler()` pops a node from `access_delayable_msg.busy_ctx` and immediately uses it via `CONTAINER_OF` without checking for NULL:

```c
sys_snode_t *node = sys_slist_get(&access_delayable_msg.busy_ctx);
struct delayable_msg_ctx *pending_msg =
        CONTAINER_OF(node, struct delayable_msg_ctx, node);

pending_msg->fired_time += 10;
```

When the busy list is empty, `sys_slist_get()` returns NULL, so `pending_msg` is also NULL (`node` is the first member of `struct delayable_msg_ctx`), and `pending_msg->fired_time += 10` performs a read-modify-write near address 0 - on Cortex-M targets this lands in the flash vector-table region and leads to a hard fault ("Bus fault on vector table read").

The issue reporter captured this deterministically on real hardware (nRF5340, BLE mesh node) during node configuration, where a data race between `bt_mesh_delayable_msg_manage()` (BT RX workqueue) and `delayable_msg_handler()` (system workqueue) - both touching the same lock-free slist with no synchronization - causes the handler to sometimes run an extra time against an already-drained busy list, hitting this exact NULL-deref path. The captured hard fault register state was byte-identical to two separate production crashes reported weeks apart.

## Fix

This applies the immediate, minimal fix the reporter proposed: add a NULL check before dereferencing. This eliminates the crash.

The underlying data race between the two execution contexts (the reporter's second, larger proposed fix - e.g. guarding the module's slists with a `k_spinlock`, or funneling both contexts through a single workqueue) is a separate, broader synchronization design question that deserves its own discussion/PR rather than being folded into this minimal crash fix.

## Verification

I don't have the nRF5340 hardware to reproduce the exact race end-to-end, so I verified the specific fix (the NULL check preventing the dereference) with a standalone C reproduction of the node-is-NULL -> `CONTAINER_OF` -> pending_msg-is-NULL -> dereference chain, confirming the pre-fix path computes a near-zero pointer that would be dereferenced, and the post-fix path returns early instead. The crash mechanism itself (NULL/near-NULL pointer dereference causing a hard fault on Cortex-M) is unambiguous from the reporter's own register dump and root-cause analysis, which I independently traced through the current upstream source to confirm still applies.

## Disclosure

Generative AI (Claude) was used to help investigate this issue, implement, and verify this fix. All changes were reviewed by me before submission.

title: net: ptp: fix 32-bit overflow in foreign clock record time window
labels: area: Networking;area: Tests;backport v3.7-branch;area: PTP;backport v4.3-branch;backport v4.4-branch
body:
`foreign_clock_cleanup()` computes the announce record aging timeout in
32-bit arithmetic before storing it into an `int64_t`. For positive
`log_msg_interval` values the product `4 * 2^log * NSEC_PER_SEC` wraps
around: with `log_msg_interval = 1` the 8 s window becomes ~3.7 s, so
announce messages still inside the window are aged out prematurely and
the port can wrongly lose its foreign time transmitter records
(Coverity CID 487738, OVERFLOW_BEFORE_WIDEN / CWE-190).

- The first commit casts the first factor to `int64_t` in both branches
  so the expression is evaluated in 64-bit arithmetic.
- The second commit adds a `foreign_master` regression test pinning the
  scaled window behavior: it fails without the fix (records dropped,
  `ptp_port_best_foreign()` returns `NULL`) and passes with it.

**Testing:** `west twister -T tests/net/ptp -p native_sim/native/64` —
all suites pass; the new test was verified to fail with the fix
reverted. `./scripts/ci/check_compliance.py` clean locally.

Fixes #84696

title: Remove non-portable bit-field layout assumptions tree-wide
body:
### Problem Description

Many places use a C bit-field struct or union to map a fixed bit layout: a hardware register, a DMA descriptor, or a wire or flash field. The C standard does not fix that layout, so this is not portable.

From: https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/blob/main/doc/contribute/coding_guidelines/index.rst?plain=1#L38
- C11 6.7.2.1: the bit order within a unit, and whether a field spills into the next unit, are implementation defined.
- Zephyr already forbids relying on this: MISRA Dir 1.1 (Required) maps to CERT EXP11-C, "Do not make assumptions regarding the layout of structures with bit-fields."

`__packed` does not help. It sets byte padding, not bit order.

Already seen in practice: [#113320](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113320) fixes a bit-field overlay in `irq_multilevel.h` that gave wrong values on big-endian. A guideline PR [#113584](https://github.com/zephyrproject-rtos/zephyr/pull/113584#discussion_r3594911198) was closed as already covered by the rule above.

A scan of `main` at `b5fb5c845b9e` (2026-07-16) finds 738 sites in 238 files. This is a wide clean-up, so it is an RFC, not one bug.

### Proposed Change (Summary)

1. Enforce the rule we already have (EXP11-C). Do not add a new rule. Replace each bit-field overlay with plain integer access using `FIELD_GET`, `FIELD_PREP`, and `GENMASK`, with byte-order helpers (`sys_le32_to_cpu` and so on) at hardware or wire boundaries.
2. Split the work by tree area. Each area is one small PR set. This issue is the tracking issue.
3. Add a CI check (checkpatch or Coccinelle) so the pattern does not come back.

No behaviour change is intended. The encodings stay the same. Only the access method changes.

The findings fall into four groups:

| Group | Meaning | Sites | Files | Confidence |
|-------|---------|------:|------:|------------|
| C1 | Direct bit-field unions | 264 | 76 | deterministic |
| C2 | Transitive bit-field unions | 38 | 32 | deterministic |
| C3 | Packed structs with bit-fields | 192 | 78 | deterministic |
| C4 | Bit-field struct over raw memory (heuristic) | 244 | 88 | heuristic, confirm each |

Sites per area:

| Area | C1 | C2 | C3 | C4 | Total |
|------|---:|---:|---:|---:|------:|
| arch | 2 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 2 |
| drivers | 132 | 6 | 79 | 175 | 392 |
| subsys | 12 | 11 | 42 | 19 | 84 |
| lib | 0 | 0 | 12 | 8 | 20 |
| soc | 87 | 2 | 8 | 4 | 101 |
| include | 29 | 16 | 46 | 0 | 91 |
| boards | 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 2 |
| tests | 0 | 3 | 0 | 37 | 40 |
| samples | 1 | 0 | 4 | 1 | 6 |
| Total | 264 | 38 | 192 | 244 | 738 |

Notes: `drivers` has the most work. `soc` is mostly register headers. `include` holds API headers owned by each subsystem. `kernel` has no findings.

### Proposed Change (Detailed)

The fix pattern:

```c
/* Before: layout is implementation defined */
union {
        uint32_t val;
        struct { uint32_t mode : 2; uint32_t vector : 8; } bits;
} reg;
reg.val      = sys_read32(ADDR);
uint8_t mode = reg.bits.mode;

/* After: portable and explicit */
#define REG_MODE   GENMASK(1, 0)
#define REG_VECTOR GENMASK(9, 2)
uint32_t reg = sys_read32(ADDR);   /* use sys_le32_to_cpu at a LE boundary */
uint8_t  mode = FIELD_GET(REG_MODE, reg);
```

Steps per PR: add named `GENMASK` masks, convert reads and writes to `FIELD_GET` and `FIELD_PREP`, add the right byte-order helper at each boundary, keep a `BUILD_ASSERT` on the word size, then remove the bit-field struct or union. Do the big-endian or cross-machine sites (protocol, DMA, flash) first.

C1 to C3 are deterministic and can be treated as a firm list. C4 is heuristic. It keeps only strong signals (register casts, casts of typed byte buffers, memcpy between a bit-field object and a byte buffer). Confirm each C4 site before its PR.

### Dependencies

This touches many maintainer areas: arch, drivers, subsys, soc, lib, include, boards, tests, and samples. See the per-area table in the summary for the size of each area. `include` headers are owned by their subsystems, not one owner. No external modules and no on-wire or on-flash encodings change. Only the access method in the code changes.

### Concerns and Unresolved Questions

- Some sites run only on little-endian GCC or Clang and work today. Do we fix all of them, or fix the big-endian, protocol, DMA, and flash sites first and treat the rest as low priority?
- C4 is heuristic. It may hold a few false positives. Confirm each before change.
- Which CI tool for the guard: checkpatch (simple) or Coccinelle (semantic)? How strict, so it does not warn on internal bit-fields where layout is never assumed?
- Scope: do we also convert reserved or padding-only fields, or only fields whose value crosses a boundary?
- Order: land the CI guard first, or the clean-up first?

### Alternatives Considered

- Do nothing and rely on the current compiler. Rejected. It breaks the adopted rule and it already broke (PR #113320).
- Byte-order guards only. Rejected. They fix endianness but not the bit order or the spill behaviour.
- Add a new coding guideline. Tried in PR #113584 and closed as already covered by MISRA Dir 1.1 and EXP11-C. So this RFC proposes enforcement, not new policy.
- Compiler-specific packing attributes. Non-standard and still do not fix the bit order.
- Use `FIELD_GET` and `FIELD_PREP` over a plain word. Chosen. Standard C, already common in the tree, same idea as Linux `linux/bitfield.h`.

Also to add, Linux documents mmap'd bitfield structs over hardware as non-portable and steers toward shift/mask instead: https://docs.kernel.org/core-api/packing.html#problem-statement (and FIELD_GET/FIELD_PREP in include/linux/bitfield.h is the concrete pattern).

Reports can be generated using the attached python script: [bitfield_layout_audit.py](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30099750/bitfield_layout_audit.py)

NOTE: Issue details and tree wide search is done using Claude Opus 4.8 LLM. Although the data is cross checked multiple time before posting here, please be aware the data could be error-prone.

title: rp2040: counter_pit_channel clock divider reset when called twice
body:
### Describe the bug

On RP2040, `counter_rpi_pico_pit_channel` counter driver can be used to manage periodic timer using PWM slice.

`counter_rpi_pico_pit_channel_set_top_value` clears the block divider to 1 (using `pwm_get_default_config` followed by `pwm_init`) before setting the correct value later when calling `pwm_set_clkdiv_int_frac`.

If we call `set_top_value` while the PWM slice is already running, we get a short time where clock divider is set to 1 which is probably not a desirable behaviour.

I noticed this while using the pit channel timer for audio playback with an external audio amplifier (through a low pass filter): when launching a second audio sample while a first was still playing I hear the second sample played much faster (expected clock divider 256 for the first sample).

Workaround: stop timer right before launching it again.

Disclosure: the source of this issue was found using Claude Sonnet 5.

- Configure a pit channel timer on rp2040 in devicetree
- Call `counter_set_top_value` and `counter_start` once
- Call `counter_set_top_value` again while the timer is still running

title: drivers: stepper: h_bridge: Propagate timing source errors
body:
`h_bridge_stepper_ctrl_move_by()` and `h_bridge_stepper_ctrl_run()` captured the timing source `update()`/`start()` return codes and logged them on failure, but then unconditionally returned `0`. Callers could not tell that the motor never started moving.

Simply returning the captured `ret` is not enough, though: the work-queue timing source did not honor the `stepper_timing_source_api` contract, which documents *0 on success, negative errno on failure*. `step_work_timing_source_start()` returned `k_work_reschedule()` verbatim (**1** when the work item is newly scheduled) and `step_work_timing_source_stop()` returned the `k_work_cancel_delayable()` flags word. So this PR fixes the timing source first, then the driver:

### 1. `drivers: stepper: gpio: honor the timing source return contract`

Normalize `step_work_timing_source_start()`/`_stop()` to return `0` on success and only propagate negative errors. The counter timing source already did this. This also fixes a latent bug in the step_dir controller, whose `stop()` treats any non-zero `timing_source->stop()` result as a failure and bails out before the pending-step accounting.

### 2. `drivers: stepper: h_bridge: Propagate timing source errors`

Return the captured error from `move_by()` and `run()`, matching what the step_dir controller does.

The commits are ordered so that each one builds and tests cleanly on its own — with the driver change alone, `drivers.stepper.stepper_ctrl.h_bridge_stepper_work_q` fails on `zassert_ok()` because `move_by()`/`run()` would return `1`.

body:

Add a -p/--parallel [N] option that runs the checks in a pool of N worker processes (one per CPU by default). Enable the new option in the compliance workflow, where the runtime of the Kconfig checks now roughly amounts to the single slowest check instead of the sum of all of them.

Full compliance check runs **2.5-3x faster** on my Mac (12 parallel processes) ; I think the performance improvement is less noticeable on Linux. **EDIT:**  just tested, on the same commit range, **Linux is roughly 5x faster** :) (16 parallel workers on this machine)

title: net: mdns_responder: fix v4_svc/v6_svc undersized for probe's resolver
body:
## Summary

`v4_svc`/`v6_svc` are shared between two different consumers:

1. The per-interface listener dispatch in `init_listener()` (needs one fd
   per interface, sized by `MDNS_MAX_IPV4/6_IFACE_COUNT`, i.e. the
   `CONFIG_NET_IF_MAX_IPV4/6_COUNT` interface-count Kconfigs).
2. When `CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER_PROBE` is enabled, `send_probe()`'s
   temporary DNS resolve context, which needs `DNS_RESOLVER_MAX_POLL`
   fds for its own server list (`DNS_RESOLVER_MAX_SERVERS` +
   `MDNS_SERVER_COUNT` + `LLMNR_SERVER_COUNT` -- at least 2 with IPv4 +
   IPv6 mDNS both enabled).

`v4_svc`/`v6_svc` were sized only for the first use. Since the
interface-count Kconfigs default to 1, any probe attempt fails
`net_socket_service_register()`'s capacity check with `-ENOMEM`
("Too many file descriptors"), and every probe silently times out --
`init_listener()` never runs, so the mDNS responder never starts at all
whenever probing is enabled with typical single-interface
configurations. The failure is invisible unless
`CONFIG_DNS_SOCKET_DISPATCHER_LOG_LEVEL_DBG` is specifically enabled
(a module nobody would think to enable while debugging a probe issue).

`net_socket_service_register()` fully replaces the previously
registered descriptor set on every call rather than accumulating (see
`cleanup_svc_events()` in `sockets_service.c`), so the two uses never
need their capacities summed -- just sized to cover whichever is
larger. This PR does exactly that: `MAX(interface count,
DNS_RESOLVER_MAX_POLL)` when probing is enabled, unchanged otherwise
to avoid wasting static memory on non-probing builds.

## Test plan

- Verified as a genuine regression, not just a plausible theory:
  reverted this change (in a local test build) and confirmed probing
  fails with `-ENOMEM` every time; restored, confirmed it works.
- No dedicated test is included in this PR: this is a sizing fix that
  `CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER_PROBE` needs to work at all, so it has no
  independently observable behavior of its own to test without also
  exercising probing end to end.
- Confirmed with a real `esp32_devkitc` ESPHome build
  (`CONFIG_MDNS_RESPONDER_PROBE` + `CONFIG_NET_DHCPV4` both on)
  compiling clean end-to-end with this fix applied.

title: posix: mutex: remove global lock from the acquisition fast path
body:
`acquire_mutex()` took a module-global semaphore on every lock, but that lock
is only needed to serialize the one-time auto-init of a statically-initialized
mutex. Pushed it into `to_posix_mutex()` (double-checked re-test) so an
already-initialized handle acquires lock-free, reading owner/type/lock_count
locklessly — exactly as `pthread_mutex_unlock()` already does.

Removes an SMP scalability bottleneck and a single-core priority-inversion window.

**Benchmark** (`qemu_cortex_a53`): 1M uncontended lock/unlock pairs drop from **817 to 508
cycles/pair (~38% fewer)**.
